Watch Megadeth’s Dave Mustaine Sniff Wine in Trailer for Family’s New Reality Show

Megadeth's Dave Mustaine and his family have a new reality show focused on making wine.

A trailer for the show recently dropped on the official YouTube channel for the family's wine business, House of Mustaine.

Mustaine Reality Show Explained

In the trailer, we see the Megadeth leader sniffing out hints of cherry in a glass of wine. There's also a clip of him checking out what appears to be grapes in a vineyard.

Outside of that, there isn't a ton of Dave to be had in the nearly eight-minute teaser.

Instead, most of the footage focuses on Dave's wife, Pamela, and daughter, Electra, as they travel and work on the family wine business.

"Once we got to Italy and couldn't speak the language, that became treacherous for me, not for her," Pamela says in one clip charting her adventures abroad with Electra.

Elsewhere, Electra draws parallels between wine-making and the world of music.

"I think House of Mustaine, being a winery, as first-generation wine makers, this project means the next chapter of the Mustaine legacy," she says. "Just like music lives on, wine lives on forever. "And that's something that we take really seriously and we hope that the future generations of the Mustaine family will want to carry as well."

What Does the Mustaine Family Know About Wine?

According to the House of Mustaine website, the family's foray into wine started when Dave performed with the San Diego Symphony in 2014. They wanted to create a wine offering that appealed to both Megadeth fans and symphony fans.

The Mustaines planted their first vines the following year. They now own vineyards in California and Italy.

READ MORE: 64 Megadeth Songs That Have Never Been Played Live

"We're not experts," Electra says in the trailer. "Well, I did become a sommelier and was one of the youngest women in America to do so, but we didn't inherit a neat little road map."

Today, House of Mustaine offers multiple wine selections named after Megadeth songs, such as:

  • Holy Wars
  • Peace Sells
  • A Tout Le Monde
  • Elysian Fields

They also offer a wine club and coordinate events such as elaborate dinners and trips to harvest grapes in Italy.

There is no indication of where the reality show will be available.

The move into wine is also notable given the work Dave Mustaine has put into his sobriety. Keep reading to hear what Dave and 24 other rockers have said about getting sober.

What 25 Rockers Have Said About Getting Sober or Quitting Drinking

Here is a look at what 25 big-name rock and metal artists have said about their sobriety journey including how they got there and what they have pledged to do with their lives since that time. 

Gallery Credit: Rob Carroll

Getty Images

Rob Halford, Judas Priest

"I have clarity now on everything, especially when it comes to my work. I'm able to perceive my music more clearly, with a lot less clutter and that's important as a musicians, particularly for me, particularly because I love what I do and I love Judas Priest so much." (GQ interview, 2020)

Getty Images

Anthony Kiedis, Red Hot Chili Peppers

"I went and I checked in and it was 30 dope fiends in the room from all walks of life, but all with a common sickness. And the counselor said, 'I'm looking at 30 of you and stats wise one of you is going to get sober out of here' Wow. And I was like, 'Get out the way because I'm taking that spot.'" (The Joe Rogan Experience via Newsweek, 2022)

Getty Images

Zakk Wylde, Black Label Society/Pantera/Ozzy Osbourne

"It's not even a matter or, 'did you shift your focus onto something else?' When I was lifting weights I'd go to the gym with a six pack, now I'm still lifting weights but I'm not drinking that. If you want to quit biting your fingernails, you just do it. It's done. You gotta go on a diet, you want to lose 15 pounds? All right, do what you gotta do. You can't be eatin' this, that or the other and then don't eat after seven every night. Just don't do it." (Metal Edge interview, 2023)

Getty Images

Slash, Guns N' Roses

"I'm not what you call a 'sobriety flag-waver,' because I am sober out of necessity more than anything. I loved a lot of the shit I used to do. But it got to a point where it wasn't fun anymore, and you couldn't recapture that high from the first time that you did it." (Yahoo Entertainment interview, 2022)

Getty Images

Kirk Hammett, Metallica

"I was spending almost every night in a nightclub or bar and then I'd spend almost every morning recovering from that. Day in, day out, regardless of whether I was on tour or not. And now that's been removed from my life I have all this extra time, so of course I'm going to play my guitar more. It's what I love to do and as a consequence of that there's just a higher output." (Kerrang! interview, 2022)

Getty Images

Nikki Sixx, Motley Crue

"People don't always understand addiction, they think we have some kinda moral affliction when the truth is we are simply allergic to drink and drugs. You are not alone. Seek others with some sober time under their belt who will understand where you're at. Isn't that what we need, to be understood?" (Facebook, 2023)

Getty Images

Ivan Moody, Five Finger Death Punch

"When I was in my fifth recovery center, Rob Halford [reached out to my manager]. He said, 'I really want to meet this gentleman, I want to know this kid. I want him to know there's somebody out there who understands.' When I was in this center, we got four phone calls a day, five minute intervals. I made it a point to call him once a day... That's one of my heroes." (Loudwire, 2022)

Getty Images

James Hetfield, Metallica

"If I want to [miss alcohol], I will. I could feed the dog that says, 'This was so great, remember this?' or I can feed the dog that says, 'Dude, look how great your life is now. Look at the crap you used to be in.' It depends how you look at it." (Far Out interview, 2022)

Getty Images

Scott Stapp, Creed

"It's hard to pick up that phone and reach out and say, 'Hey, I am struggling. I need somebody right now.' That's something that really, really hindered me when I first started trying to get sober in 2008. I would never pick up the phone. I was white-knuckling it and just for some reason, the phone was 10,000 pounds." (People, 2024)

Getty Images

Corey Taylor, Slipknot

"The first few years is weird, because you realize quickly how much a part of your personality booze has become. You kind of have to sort out who you are, what you're comfortable with and largely just the habit of it." (The Moon Under Water podcast via NME, 2022)

Getty Images

Dave Mustaine, Megadeth

"It's a funny thing, we had this saying, 'Getting sober is like having sex with a gorilla. You're not done until the gorilla is done.' Some of use wanted to get clean and then the others didn't. Then one guy would show and he'd be clean, the other guys would be loaded. Then he'd see the other guy loaded, and go, 'Eh, fuck it! I'm in!' And then he'd get loaded, too. It was just like whack-a-mole with all of us with our bad behavior." (Forbes interview, 2020)

Getty Images

Ace Frehley, ex-KISS

"Every time I perform a concert I usually have meet-and-greets after the show. At least one person comes up to me and says. 'Ace, I've been sober two years,' 'Ace, I've been sober five years.' I'm helping people live longer lives, more fruitful lives, because I'm a power of example. Go figure." (Trunk Nation with Eddie Trunk interview via Blabbermouth.net)

Getty Images

Jonathan Davis, Korn

"I got sober right after we did the third record. So I stopped meth when we started touring because I couldn't function. There's no way I could be up for two days and tour and keep it together and I had to stop. So the day we took off on tour, the first tour with House Of Pain and Biohazard, we got in our trailer and we built bunks and I just got on that bunk and I slept for five fucking days, got up and played a show and that's when I kicked it." (Wild Ride! podcast interview via Alternative Press, 2020)

Getty Images

Tommy Lee, Motley Crue

"I was drinking two gallons (of vodka) — not pints, not — gallons, the big handles, a day... I just became sort of immune to it and realized, 'Whoa, this is a lot. Like, this isn't good.' So it was time for me to pump the brakes and, you know, just — just get rid of it for a while. I don't know if it's a forever thing. But for now, I'm not drinking vodka today." (Yahoo Entertainment interview, 2020)

Getty Images

Jacoby Shaddix, Papa Roach

"As I peeled away all the things that I medicated myself with, I was left with me – and I wasn't happy with that I was left with. I had to really take some time to rebuild who I was, who I am and who I'm becoming. It's always a work in progress." (Spin interview, 2022)

Getty Images

Duff McKagan, Guns N' Roses

"I realized I was self-medicating when I got sober. So I was like 'Now what dod I do with these panic attacks?' That's where martial arts came in. I met my sensei, who is still my sensei and I saw the calmness in his eyes. I was like, 'If I could get that, I wonder if I could handle my panic attacks better.'" (People interview, 2023)

Getty Images

Deryck Whibley, Sum 41

"Everything was just starting from zero. I was terrified that first year. I never created music while drinking, but I used to believe that having the excitement of going out and partying made me creative." (People interview, 2024)

Getty Images

Randy Blythe, Lamb of God

"I used to get upset thinking about wasting time fucking drinking, but since I got sober my brain has been on overdrive and my creative output has quintupled. I used to get upset about that, but there's no reason to sit in despair over thing you could have done. You just have to start doing things now." (Kerrang! interview, 2020)

Getty Images

Jerry Cantrell, Alice In Chains

"The hardest thing is to help yourself and, you know, I think a lot of part of achieving sobriety and maintaining sobriety is keeping yourself open to be of service and to be of help to somebody in need. Because you know how hard it is to make those first initial steps and if you're the guy to stick around." (Maximum Firepower podcast via AlternativeNation.net)

Getty Images

Andreas Kisser, Sepultura

"I realized I was a slave to alcohol. Every situation where I had to choose a restaurant or what type of traveling I would do with my family, what kind of social thing we'd go to, alcohol was the biggest element to make the choices ... I realized I was losing myself because of that idea [and the] choices [I was making]." (RockSverige via Loudwire, 2021)

Getty Images

Mike McCready, Pearl Jam

"Once I cleaned up, I couldn't play for a week and a half. I'd been used to being screwed up and playing ... It was a psychological thing." (Spokane Spokesman-Review interview, 1995)

Getty Images

Billie Joe Armstrong, Green Day

"There's a lot more sober people – I've noticed that and maybe because I was the only one that was hammered before, that now I notice that people are more sober now and it was just something I was unaware of, because I was shitfaced or something." (People interview, 2024)

Getty Images

David Ellefson, Megadeth

"When I got sober in 1990, it took a year until people would trust me because I was always letting them down. The 18 months before that – starting with Monsters of Rock in Donington 1988 – were incredibly dark. That's why Download (festival) for me is a moment where everything gets brought back home: playing the biggest shows of my life, but in my worst condition due to being a heroin addict. Every time we've played since is a chance to make amends." (Metal Hammer, 2022)

Getty Images

Alice Cooper

"Alice was different. He was not going to be the whipping boy of society anymore. He was going to be this new, reborn villain. He was going to stand up straight, he was going to look the audience int he eye, he was going to be in control. The new, sober Alice was much more dangerous than the old Alice." (Classic Rock interview, 2023)

Getty Images

Trent Reznor, Nine Inch Nails

"There was an awkward adjustment of learning how to live without [drugs and alcohol], without those things, those people, those crutches and habits. Once I got on stable ground and started to understand how my brain worked without all that, musically at least, I can do more because I can remember what I did. I can think deeper about things." (Kerrang! interview, 2017)
